Pd-Catalyzed Dearomative Asymmetric Allylic Alkylation of
Naphthols with Alkoxyallenes
Jinjin Hu, Shulei Pan, Shuai Zhu, Peiyuan Yu, Ruigang Xu, Guofu Zhong, and Xiaofei Zeng *
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2020, 85, 7896 −7904 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A Pd-catalyzed linear selective intermolecular
asymmetric dearomative allylic alkylation reaction of naphthols
with alkoxyallenes under mild reaction conditions is reported. The
transformation is successfully promoted by Pd
2(dba)3 and the
chiral Trost ligand and provides a general atom-e ﬃcient protocol
to obtain various β-naphthalenones bearing an all carbon
quaternary stereogenic center in good yields and chemo- and
stereoselectivities.
■ INTRODUCTION
Cyclohexadienones with ortho-quaternary carbon centers
constitute the main structural elements of many natural
products1 and biologically active compounds. 2 Thus, tremen-
dous attention from synthetic chemists has been received for
the construction of a cyclohexadienone skeleton.
3 In recent
years, the transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric dearomative
allylic substitution reactions 4 have been proven to be one of
the most e ﬃcient strategies for preparing target molecules
from simple phenols or naphthols. 5 A series of successful
examples have been realized by using allylic alcohol 6 and their
derivatives7 as the π-allylic precursors ( Scheme 1 a). To
improve the atom economy, Lin and co-workers reported a
redox-neutral strategy for the dearomative coupling of β-
naphthols with alkynes via Pd hydride catalysis, providing the
desired naphthalenones in good yields.
8 Later on, Yang and co-
workers disclosed a highly e ﬃcient palladium-catalyzed direct
oxidative allylic C −H dearomatization of 2-naphthols to access
naphthalenones.9 Despite the impressive advances in dear-
omative allylic substitution of naphthols, exploring new types
of electrophiles to enrich the application scope of these
transformations is still challenging and highly desirable. In this
regard, Bandini and co-workers reported gold(I)-catalyzed
dearomatization of 2-naphthols with allenamides in high yields
and selectivities.
10 The asymmetric version of this reaction was
then reported by Shao and co-workers by using chiral Brønsted
acid catalysis, a ﬀording the target allylic dearomatization
products in good to excellent enantioselectivities. 11
With the pioneering reports by Trost and co-workers, 12
alkoxyallenes have been widely employed as useful π-allyl
fragment precursors for transit ion-metal-catalyzed allylic
addition reactions to pronucleophiles, and considerable
interest has been received from synthetic chemists due to
the highly branched reg ioselectivity and e ﬃcient atom
economy.
13 Numerous soft 14 and hard 15 nucleophiles have
been involved in this reaction during the last decade. In line
with our interest in the development of catalytically

asymmetric dearomatic reactions of naphthols 6b and selectiv-
ity-controllable allylic substitution reactions, 16 we assumed that
an asymmetric metal-catalyzed intermolecular nucleophilic
addition reaction to alkoxyallenes involving π-allyl intermedi-
ates would be highly suitable for β-naphthols, allowing access
to dearomative cyclohexadienone derivatives. Herein, we
report the ﬁrst Pd-catalyzed linear selective asymmetric allylic
dearomatization of β-naphthols with alkoxyallenes for the
construction of β-naphthalenones bearing an all-carbon
quaternary chiral center in good yields and enantioselectivities.
Interestingly, α-naphthols were also found to be suitable
substrates in this reaction system.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We initiated our study by using 1,3-(Me) 2-naphthyl-2-ol ( 1a)
and alkoxyallenes ( 2a) as the model substrates to optimize the
reaction conditions. The initial test was performed in the
presence of 2.5 mol % Pd(dba)
2, 5 mol % ligand ( R)-L117 as
the catalyst, 1.0 equiv of DBU as the base, and dicholoroethane
(DCE) as solvent, and the reaction proceeded smoothly with
high conversion of 1a. Interestingly, a linear selective product
(3a) was formed in a 64% yield and 55:45 e.r. ( Table 1, entry
1). Encouraged by this positive result, we then screened a
series of ligands, and the Trost ligand ( R,R)-L5 proved to be
the best with respect to enantioselectivities and yields for the
model reaction ( Table 1 , entry 5). Taking ( R,R)-L5 as the
optimal ligand, di ﬀerent palladium precursors such as
Pd
2(dba)3,P d 2(dba)3CHCl3, and Pd(OAc) 2 were tested, and
Pd2(dba) 3 was found to be the best, furnishing the
corresponding product in a 66% yield and 89:11 e.r. ( Table
1, entry 6). On further optimizing the reaction conditions by
varying the solvent, base, and reaction temperature (for details,
see the Supporting Information, Table S1 ), we identi ﬁed the
following optimal conditions: 1a (0.2 mmol) was treated with
2a (1.5 equiv) in the presence of Pd 2(dba)3 (2.5 mol %),
(R,R)-L5 (5 mol %), and DBU (1.0 equiv) in propylene oxide
(PO, 0.1 M) at 60 °C for 12 h, and 3a (E/Z > 19:1) was
obtained in an 81% yield with 92:8 e.r. ( Table 1 , entry 11).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we
investigated the substrate scope of this dearomative asym-
metric allylic alkylation process ( Scheme 2 ). Alkoxyallenes
bearing di ﬀerent electron-withdrawing or electron-donating
groups on the phenyl ring underwent the reaction smoothly,
delivering the corresponding β-naphthalenones in high yields
and good stereoselectivities. ( 3b−3l, 60−92% yields, 91:9 −
93.5:6.5 e.r. ’s). Gratifyingly, β-naphthols with di ﬀerent
substitution groups at 1- or 3-positions, such as allyl, alkyl,
and methyl groups, were also well tolerated in the reaction,
giving 3m−3t in good yields and enantioselectivities. (61 −89%
yield, 92.5:7.5 −94.5:5.5 e.r. ’s). Furthermore, 1,3-dimethyl-6-
phenylnaphthalen-2-ol ( 1u) was also a good substrate,
providing the desired dearomative product 3u with a good
yield and enantioselectivity. To con ﬁrm the absolute
conﬁguration (AC) of the products, ECD spectra were
calculated by the TD-DFT method, which has been proven
to be useful in predicting ECD spectra and assigning the AC of
organic molecules. The R conﬁguration could be reliably
assigned to compound 3a (see Figure S1 in the Supporting
Information).
Next, we examined the compatibility of our reaction
protocol with α-naphthols under standard conditions. As
shown in Scheme 3 , 2-allylnaphth-1-ols with di ﬀerent
substitution groups react with di ﬀerent alkoxyallenes smoothly,
giving the desired chiral α-naphthalenones (5a−5f) with good

yields (up to a 79% yield) and enantioselectivities (up to 94:6
e.r.). To demonstrate the utility of the Pd-catalyzed
asymmetric dearomatization reaction of naphthols, prepara-
tive-scale synthesis of 3a was carried out to e ﬃciently a ﬀord
1.81 g of 3a in a 78% yield and 92:8 e.r. ( Scheme 4 a). There
was almost no change in either the yield or enantioselectivity,
suggesting that large-scale chemical production of chiral
naphthalenones may be feasible. Diastereoselective reduction
of the ketone group of 3a with NaBH
4 gave alcohol 3ab in a
95% yield with 95:5 d.r. and 91.5:8.5 e.r. ( Scheme 4 b).
To gain insight into the reaction mechanism, we performed
several control experiments. First, the dearomatization reaction
was carried out under standard conditions without the base,
and it was found that both yields and enantioselectivities were
decreased (31% yield and 60:40 e.r.) ( Scheme 4 c). This
outcome indicated that the L*Pd(II)−H species II generated
from the chiral palladium complex with naphthol ( 1a) could
react with allene ( 2a) automatically without a base and,
however, the reaction is too slow, which resulted in a low yield.
In addition, 2-methoxy-1,3-dimethylnaphthalene (MeO- 1a)
could not proceed in the reaction at all ( Scheme 4 d). Then, a
deuterium-labeling experiment was carried out by adding 1
drop of D
2O in the reaction under standard conditions. It
could be seen that 61% of the H atoms at the middle carbon of
allene was deuterated. ( Scheme 4 e) Based on these
experimental results and previous related work, 18 a possible
catalytical cycle was proposed. First, an oxidative addition of
L*Pd(0) I, in situ generated from Pd
2(dba)3 with a chiral
ligand ( L*), to the naphthol ( 1a) generates L*Pd(II)−H
species II, which can e ﬃciently prohibit the O-position from
attacking the allene moiety. 15c Then, the hydropalladation of II
with allene ( 2a) forms a transition state III, and III will
facilitate the nucleophilic addition of the naphthol to the π-allyl
fragment, allowing access to the desired linear product
enantioselectively through a reductive elimination process
(Scheme 5 ).
■ CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed a Pd-catalyzed dearomative
asymmetric allylic alkylation reaction of naphthols with
alkoxyallenes. Both α- and β-naphthols were well tolerated in
the reaction and provided various α- and β-naphthalenones
bearing an all carbon quaternary center in good yields (up to
95%) and enantioselectivities (up to 94.5:5.5 e.r.) with good
functional-group tolerance. The catalytic process involved the
hydropalladation of alkoxyallene and subsequent allyl sub-

desired products in absolutely linear selectivity. This approach
provides a concise route for access to enantiomeric enriched
naphthalenones.

General Information. Analytical thin layer chromatography
(TLC) was performed using a Merck 60F254 precoated silica gel
plate (0.2 mm in thickness). Subsequent to elution, plates were
visualized using UV radiation (254 nm) on Spectroline Model ENF-
24061/F of 254 nm. Further visualization was possible by staining
with a basic solution of potassium permanganate or acidic solution of
ceric molybdate. Flash column chromatography was performed using
Merck aluminum oxide90 active, neutral with freshly distilled solvents.
Columns were typically packed as slurry and equilibrated with the
appropriate solvent system prior to use. Proton nuclear magnetic
resonance spectra (
1H NMR) were recorded on a Bruker AMX 500
spectrophotometer (CDCl 3 as solvent). Chemical shifts for 1H NMR
spectra are reported as δ in units of parts per million (ppm) down ﬁeld
from SiMe 4 (0.0) and relative to the signal of chloroform- d (7.26,
singlet). Multiplicities were given as s (singlet), d (doublet), t
(triplet), dd (doublets of doublet), or m (multiplets). The number of
protons ( n) for a given resonance is indicated by nH. Coupling
constants are reported as a J value in hertz. Carbon nuclear magnetic
resonance spectra ( 13C NMR) are reported as δ in units of parts per
million (ppm) down ﬁeld from SiMe 4 (0.0) and relative to the signal
of chloroform- d (77.0, triplet). Enantiomeric excesses were
determined by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)
analysis on a chiral stationary phase, CHIRALCEL IC, CHIRALCEL
OD, or CHIRALCEL AD. Optical rotations were measured in CHCl 3
on a Schmidt + Haensdchpolarimeter (Polartronic MH8) with a 10
cm cell ( c given in g/100 mL). High-resolution mass spectrometry
(HRMS) was recorded on a QTOF Premier for ESI+. The racemic
products used to determine the ee values were synthesized by using
Pd(PPh
3)4 as the catalyst. The starting materials 1 and 2 were
prepared according to the literature reported. 19
